name: Nehemiah

objectives.text: Identify Nehemiah as the cupbearer who served the king of Persia
Retell that Nehemiah led God's people to rebuild the broken walls of Jerusalem
Recall that the builders worked with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other
Describe how Nehemiah prayed to God before he answered the king's question
Summarize how Nehemiah organized the people so that each group repaired a section of the wall, often near its own house
Explain why an ancient city needed walls and why Jerusalem's broken walls were a disgrace to God's people
Describe how the people listened, wept, and then rejoiced when Ezra read the Law aloud
Identify the parts of Nehemiah's prayer in chapter 1, including praise, confession of sin, remembering God's promise, and making a request
Locate Susa and Jerusalem on a map and describe Nehemiah's journey from the Persian court to Judah
Describe how the people dedicated the finished wall with thanksgiving, singing, and great joy
Identify Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem and describe the tactics of mockery, threats, and deception they used against the work
Explain how Nehemiah answered opposition by both praying to God and setting a guard
Outline the book of Nehemiah in two main movements, the rebuilding of the wall and the renewal of the people
Explain how the book shows God's providence working through a pagan king and through the swift completion of the wall
Describe Nehemiah's leadership actions, such as inspecting the walls, casting vision, organizing workers, and refusing the governor's food allowance, citing the text for each
Analyze the economic injustice described in Nehemiah 5 and explain how Nehemiah's response applied the Law's teaching on lending to the poor
Place Nehemiah's mission in the Persian period under Artaxerxes I and explain how it followed the earlier returns under Zerubbabel and Ezra
Interpret the statement that the joy of the LORD is your strength in its context of hearing the Law and keeping the feast
Explain how the Levites read the Law clearly and gave its sense so the people understood, and relate this to the Reformed teaching on the reading and preaching of the Word
Analyze the prayer of confession in Nehemiah 9 as a retelling of Israel's history that contrasts God's faithfulness with the people's repeated rebellion
Explain how the public reading of the Law led to confession and a written covenant pledge, and list the specific commitments the people made
Compare the roles of Nehemiah as governor and Ezra as priest and scribe in the restoration community
Explain that Ezra and Nehemiah form one book in the Hebrew canon and describe how Nehemiah's first-person memoir and its lists shape the book
Explain Nehemiah's Sabbath reform and relate it to the fourth commandment as the Reformed confessions teach it
Construct a profile of godly leadership from Nehemiah that weighs both his strengths and his faults, supported with textual evidence
Evaluate whether the reforms lasted by comparing the covenant pledges of chapter 10 with the failures Nehemiah found in chapter 13
Analyze Nehemiah's recurring prayers for God to remember him and what they show about his reliance on God's steadfast love
Evaluate how the unresolved ending of Nehemiah points beyond itself to the need for the new covenant fulfilled in Christ
Compose an essay tracing how prayer and practical action work together throughout the book of Nehemiah in light of the Reformed doctrine of God working through means

changes: Kept and reworded real competencies (cupbearer, wall, tool and sword, prayer before the king, organizing builders, why walls mattered, Ezra comparison, usury, opposition, Law and covenant renewal, leadership profile, durability of reforms, prayer and action). Replaced the vague 'apply leadership skills' with a text-cited description of leadership actions, recast 'significance of Jerusalem' as the disgrace of the broken walls, and turned the topography research into a map task at an earlier grade. Added missing content: the structure of Nehemiah's chapter 1 prayer, the dedication of the wall, God's providence, book outline, Persian-period setting, the joy of the LORD in context, the Levites explaining the Law, the chapter 9 confession, the covenant pledge details, the canonical unity of Ezra-Nehemiah, the Sabbath reform, the 'remember me' prayers, and the book's pointing forward to the new covenant. Anchored objectives to specific verses and Westminster standards where they state the doctrine.
